h.en: 5.1 Wall footing and column footing — the sketching set
h.gu: 5.1 Wall footing and column footing — the sketching set

items.syllabus_item: 5.1 Draw sketches: Wall and column footing (incl. 200 mm and 300 mm thick wall foundation of the practical list)

body.en:
Component thinking. Unit 3 placed foundations in buildings; this unit isolates each component as a sketchable standard: given a wall or a column, you must produce its footing section from memory with sizes, materials and levels. These are the A3-sketchbook practicals of the syllabus.

Wall (strip) footing — construction from below. On levelled, watered and rammed trench bottom: PCC bed 75–100 mm (1:4:8/1:5:10) projecting 100–150 mm each side → stepped footing in brick/stone masonry, 2–3 steps, each step height a course multiple (≈200 mm brick) and offset ≈50 mm per side, widening wall→required width → masonry continues to plinth → DPC 40–50 mm rich concrete/mortar (or bituminous system) full wall width → wall above. Foundation depth usually 900–1200 mm below ground to firm, season-stable soil for house loads; width by load/SBC (Numerical 3.2's method).

200 mm and 300 mm walls — what changes. The steps scale with the wall: a 200 mm (partition/light) wall takes a narrower footing (commonly 500–600 mm bottom step), a 300 mm (heavy/external in older stone/brick practice) wall a wider one (700–900 mm); offsets stay ≈50 mm so the number of steps grows with width. In sketches state: wall thickness, each step's width/height, bed width/thickness and depth — a footing sketch without sizes is a picture, not a drawing.

Column (isolated) footing. RCC pad — plain rectangular, sloped-top or stepped — with bottom mesh both ways, 50 mm cover on PCC, column starter bars bent into it, size/depth from the structural design (residential G+1 pads commonly 1.2–1.8 m square, 300–500 deep at edge thick— design governs). Plinth/tie beam at top connects columns, carries ground walls and resists differential settlement. Eccentric/combined footings appear at boundaries (Unit 3).

Sketch checklist (both). GL line with hatching below (earth side), foundation level/depth dimension, every width in a dimension chain below, materials labelled (PCC/masonry/RCC), DPC in wall footing only, column bars in column footing only. Section is cut through the middle; plan of a column footing shows the square pad dashed under the column grid (Unit 3).

items.syllabus_item: 5.1 Draw sketches: floors and floorings, false ceiling

body.en:
Floor = structure + finish. A ground floor is built on earth; an upper floor is a slab. The sketch names both layers: base (what carries) and flooring (what you walk on, chosen for wear, water, appearance).

Ground floor build-up (bottom up). Compacted earth filling (150–300, in layers, watered) → soling/PCC base 75–100 (or lean concrete over rubble soling in older practice) → DPC/waterproof layer where damp threatens (always under wet-area finishes) → bedding 20–30 mortar/sand → finish. Wet areas add: slope 1:60–1:100 to the nahani trap, waterproof coating turned 300 up skirting. Section shows every thickness — total floor build-up sets plinth/floor levels for the whole plan (Unit 3 sections inherit it).

Flooring types (sketch + one-line duty). Cement concrete/IPS (Indian patent stone): cheap, hard, repairable — workshops, stores, under-finish base. Terrazzo (mosaic): chips in cement, ground polished — traditional houses, schools. Tiles — ceramic/vitrified/porcelain: factory finish, sizes 300×300 to 600×600+, wet-laid or adhesive, skirting 100–150. Stone — kota/marble/granite: durable slabs on mortar bed, polished in place. Wooden/parquet and vinyl/laminate: dry-laid finishes over a level base, comfort rooms. Choice follows room duty: water rooms need non-absorbent, sloped finishes; living rooms trade on appearance and maintenance (Unit Drawing economy principle in material form).

Upper floors. RCC slab (Card 5.5) + bedding + finish as above; bathrooms on upper floors demand waterproofing sandwich and sunken slab (typically 150–300 sunken) for plumbing — the section must show the sunken zone, filling (lightweight) and trap levels, a favourite exam sketch.

False ceiling. A light secondary ceiling suspended below the slab: metal grid (GI/aluminium channels) on hangers 150–600 below slab, boards/panels (gypsum, calcium-silicate, mineral fibre, metal tiles) fixed at chosen level. Duties: hide services (ducts, cables, pipes), improve acoustics and thermal feel, carry recessed lights, lower room height visually. Sketch: slab, hanger, main + cross channels, board, pelmet/light trough, and the minimum clear height bye-law cheek (false ceiling may not steal the required room height). Access panels for service points must be drawn, not wished.

items.syllabus_item: 5.1 Draw sketches: roofs and roof coverings

body.en:
Roof duties. Shed rain, resist sun/wind, insulate, and carry its covering for decades. Form follows span and climate; the sketch set is: pitched, flat and curved/shell, each with its covering system.

Pitched (sloping) roofs. Timber/steel trusses or rafters on wall plates; forms: lean-to (verandah), gable, hip, gambrel/mansard (recognise). Slope by covering: Mangalore tiles ≈ 30–35°, AC/GI sheets ≈ 15–25° (manufacturer/lap governs), shingles/slates steeper. Coverings: Mangalore/clay tiles on battens; corrugated GI or aluminium sheets on purlins; asbestos-cement (legacy — health hazard in modern specification; fibre-cement successors used); stone slabs on close battens in hill practice. Sketch shows: rafter/purlin/batten order, ridge, eaves with gutter, gable infill, and ceiling below where provided. Valleys and hips collect water — flashing lines belong on the sketch.

Flat roofs. RCC slab as roof with a terrace system: slope 1:100–1:120 laid in the waterproofing/terracing (brickbat coba or foam-concrete with tile finish in Indian practice), rainwater outlets at low corners with khurras and downpipes, parapet 600–900 with coping and drip. The section (slab → slope layer → finish, parapet junction waterproofing turned up) is the examinable sketch: most roof leaks are drawn wrong at junctions before they are built wrong.

Curved/shell and special roofs. Thin RCC shells, domes, folded plates: form gives strength, covering is the shell plus waterproof coating; north-light (sawtooth) trusses for factories. Recognise and sketch the profile with supports; design is beyond this subject.

Common vocabulary for sketches. Ridge (top), eaves (bottom edge), gable (triangle wall), hip (sloping corner), valley (inner corner), purlin (mid support), rafter, batten, wall plate, fascia, gutter, flashing, coping, khurra (terrace drain mouth). Label at least six on any roof sketch — vocabulary is marks.

body.en:
Every opening = frame + shutter(s) + ironmongery. The frame is fixed to masonry (holdfasts in mortar/concrete), the shutter moves or glazes. Sketches are elevations + a section through jamb/sill so sizes of members can be read.

Doors — types to sketch (any two well). Ledged-battened: vertical battens held by horizontal ledges + diagonal brace — cheap, sheds/stores. Framed-panelled: stiles/rails frame with raised panels — the standard house door (diagram). Flush: flat-faced (ply/blockboard core) — modern interiors, offices. Glazed/partly glazed: light with privacy balance. Sliding, folding, revolving, rolling shutter and collapsible: special duties (shops/garages/entrances) — recognise forms. Member data: frame ≈ 100×75 to 125×75; shutter 30–40 thick; door sizes from the schedule (D1 1000×2100 main, D2 900×2000/2100, D3 750×2000 bath — Unit 3 table).

Windows — types. Casement: side-hung shutters opening out/in (diagram) — full ventilation, the house standard. Fixed + casement combos, bay windows (projecting, prospect), sliding (aluminium/uPVC, no swing space), louvred (ventilation with privacy — stores/bath), pivoted and sash (double-hung) (recognise). Frame ≈ 100×75 reduced for windows; shutters glazed (glass panes in putty/beading) with grills on the inner face for security in residential practice. Sill ≈ 750–900 above floor for rooms (sitting sight-line), lintel level common 2100 so door/window tops align across the elevation.

Ventilators. Small high openings (sill ≈ 1800, sizes ≈ 600×450) above doors/windows or independent: fixed/adjustable louvres or glass slats, for hot-air escape and privacy ventilation (bath-WC, kitchen, stores). In the elevation, the ventilator-over-door combined unit is a stock sketch; in plan it shares the window-type symbol.

Drawing an opening completely. Elevation (frame, shutter division, opening direction lines — diagonal cross lines on glazed/fixed panes as your office convention states), section (frame in wall, sill slope/throating to throw water, lintel above, chajja outside), member sizes and the schedule symbol tying sheet to table (D2/W1/V). An opening drawn without its symbol is unscheduled — and unscheduled means unestimated.

h.en: 5.5 Beam and slab reinforcement — reading the steel
h.gu: 5.5 Beam and slab reinforcement — reading the steel

items.syllabus_item: 5.1 Draw sketches: beam and slab reinforcement (with Unit 3.2.3 RCC details)

body.en:
The principle in one line. Concrete takes compression, steel takes tension — so steel is placed where the member is pulled: bottom at mid-span, top over supports, top throughout a cantilever. Every sketch in this card is that sentence drawn.

Beam — longitudinal section. Main bottom bars running between supports, bent up (cranked) near ends in older detailing or continued with separate top support bars in modern detailing; top (hanger/support) bars; stirrups as vertical links wrapping the bars — spacing closer near supports (shear maximum), wider mid-span; side bars when depth is large. Cross-section shows the cage: bars as dots, stirrup as the closed link, width × effective depth, cover 25 mm marked by the gap between stirrup and concrete face.

Slab — plan and sections. One-way (supported on two opposite sides, L/B ≥ 2): main bars along the short span at bottom, distribution bars perpendicular above them (temperature/shrinkage + load spread), top steel over supports by bent-up bars or separate mats. Two-way (L/B < 2): main steel both ways, corner care per design. Show bar spacing (e.g., 8 ∅ @ 150 c/c), slab thickness (100–125 residential), cover 15–20, and trimmers around the stair/duct openings (Unit 3).

How to read a bar note. '10 ∅ @ 130 c/c' = 10 mm diameter bars at 130 mm centres. A bar mark (B1, T2…) keys the drawing to the bar-bending schedule: shape, length, number. On sketches, write mark + size + spacing beside the member, never floating.

Site truth the drawing prevents. Chajja built with bottom steel collapses at casting; slab top steel walked flat by labour loses support strength; stirrups spread evenly because 'spacing was not drawn' wastes steel mid-span and starves supports. The reinforcement sketch is safety in pencil — draw spacing zones, covers and laps explicitly.

Companion sketches of 5.1 (one-line duties). Floors (5.2), roofs (5.3), false ceiling (5.2), doors/windows/ventilators (5.4), footings (5.1) complete the syllabus list; examiners rotate through them as 'draw a neat sketch of…', so each component must be producible as one clean labelled section/elevation without notes to hide behind.

title.en: Numerical 5.1 — Flooring quantity for a room (tiles + skirting)
title.gu: Numerical 5.1 — Flooring quantity for a room (tiles + skirting)

body.en:
Given. Room 4.2 m × 3.6 m (internal). Vitrified tiles 600 × 600 mm. Skirting height 100 mm on all walls; deduct one door 900 mm from skirting. Add 5% for cutting/breakage.

Find. Number of tiles to order and skirting length.

Step 1. Find the floor area.

floor area = 4.2 × 3.6 = 15.12 m²

Step 2. Find one tile's area and the tiles needed.

one tile = 0.6 × 0.6 = 0.36 m² ; tiles = 15.12 / 0.36 = 42.0 → 42 tiles

Step 3. Add the cutting/breakage allowance.

order = 42 × 1.05 = 44.1 → 45 tiles (practically: round to full boxes)

Step 4. Find the skirting length.

perimeter = 2 × (4.2 + 3.6) = 15.6 m ; skirting = 15.6 − 0.9 = 14.7 m at 100 mm height

Final answer.

╔ Order 45 tiles (600×600) and 14.7 m of 100 mm skirting ╗

Validity check. Check by grid: 4.2/0.6 = 7 tiles × 3.6/0.6 = 6 tiles = 42 exact — an even module; non-module rooms raise cutting waste above 5%, which is why the allowance is stated on the estimate, not hidden.

Validity check. Check by grid: 4.2/0.6 = 7 tiles × 3.6/0.6 = 6 tiles = 42 exact — an even module; non-module rooms raise cutting waste above 5%, which is why the allowance is stated on the estimate, not hidden.

title.en: Numerical 5.2 — Door/window schedule count and glass area
title.gu: Numerical 5.2 — Door/window schedule count and glass area

body.en:
Given. A floor has: D1 1000×2100 (1 no., fully panelled), D2 900×2000 (4 nos.), W1 1200×1200 glazed windows (5 nos., assume 75% of window area is glass after frame/shutters), V 600×450 ventilators (3 nos., fully louvred). Find total glass area and total door shutter area.

Step 1. Window glass: find one window's area, then glass portion.

one W1 = 1.2 × 1.2 = 1.44 m² ; glass per window = 0.75 × 1.44 = 1.08 m²

Step 2. Multiply by the number of windows.

total glass = 5 × 1.08 = 5.40 m²

Step 3. Door shutter area (use opening size as first estimate).

D1 area = 1.0 × 2.1 = 2.10 m² ; D2 area = 4 × (0.9 × 2.0) = 7.20 m² ; total = 9.30 m²

Final answer.

╔ Glass ≈ 5.40 m² ; door shutters ≈ 9.30 m² (frames measured separately by length) ╗

Validity check. This is how the schedule of openings (Unit 3) becomes an estimate: count × size per symbol. Louvred ventilators contribute no glass; if a ventilator were glazed, its 0.27 m² each would join Step 2.

q.en: Draw/describe the section of a wall footing for a 230 mm wall.
q.gu: Draw/describe the section of a wall footing for a 230 mm wall.

a.en: PCC bed (75-100, projecting 100-150 per side) - 2-3 stepped masonry offsets of about 50 mm per side widening to the footing width - masonry to plinth - 40-50 mm DPC - wall above; depth 900-1200 mm to firm soil.
a.gu: PCC bed (75-100, projecting 100-150 per side) - 2-3 stepped masonry offsets of about 50 mm per side widening to the footing width - masonry to plinth - 40-50 mm DPC - wall above; depth 900-1200 mm to firm soil.

q.en: Why does a column footing have steel mesh both ways?
q.gu: Why does a column footing have steel mesh both ways?

a.en: A column delivers a point load; the pad bends in both directions as it spreads the load to the soil, so main steel runs both ways (with 50 mm cover).
a.gu: A column delivers a point load; the pad bends in both directions as it spreads the load to the soil, so main steel runs both ways (with 50 mm cover).

q.en: Name the layers of a ground floor from bottom.
q.gu: Name the layers of a ground floor from bottom.

a.en: Compacted filling - PCC/soling base - DPC/waterproof layer where needed - bedding - finish (tile/stone/IPS), with slope to trap in wet areas.
a.gu: Compacted filling - PCC/soling base - DPC/waterproof layer where needed - bedding - finish (tile/stone/IPS), with slope to trap in wet areas.

q.en: What is a false ceiling and why is it provided?
q.gu: What is a false ceiling and why is it provided?

a.en: A light ceiling suspended below the slab on a metal grid: hides services, improves acoustics/thermal feel, carries lights. Access panels are needed at service points.
a.gu: A light ceiling suspended below the slab on a metal grid: hides services, improves acoustics/thermal feel, carries lights. Access panels are needed at service points.

q.en: State suitable roof slopes: Mangalore tiles vs corrugated sheets.
q.gu: State suitable roof slopes: Mangalore tiles vs corrugated sheets.

a.en: Mangalore tiles about 30-35 degrees; corrugated GI/AC-type sheets about 15-25 degrees (covering manufacturer's lap rules govern).
a.gu: Mangalore tiles about 30-35 degrees; corrugated GI/AC-type sheets about 15-25 degrees (covering manufacturer's lap rules govern).

q.en: Difference between a door frame and shutter; give frame size.
q.gu: Difference between a door frame and shutter; give frame size.

a.en: Frame is fixed to the wall (about 100×75 to 125×75 mm) and carries the shutter; the shutter (30-40 mm) is the moving/closing leaf.
a.gu: Frame is fixed to the wall (about 100×75 to 125×75 mm) and carries the shutter; the shutter (30-40 mm) is the moving/closing leaf.

q.en: Why is a ventilator placed high, near the ceiling?
q.gu: Why is a ventilator placed high, near the ceiling?

a.en: Hot air rises; a high opening (sill about 1800) lets it escape while keeping privacy - standard over bath-WC and kitchens.
a.gu: Hot air rises; a high opening (sill about 1800) lets it escape while keeping privacy - standard over bath-WC and kitchens.

q.en: In a slab, what is distribution steel for?
q.gu: In a slab, what is distribution steel for?

a.en: Perpendicular to main bars: spreads load, ties the main bars at spacing, and resists shrinkage/temperature cracking.
a.gu: Perpendicular to main bars: spreads load, ties the main bars at spacing, and resists shrinkage/temperature cracking.

q.en: Where are stirrups closest in a beam, and why?
q.gu: Where are stirrups closest in a beam, and why?

a.en: Near the supports - shear force is maximum there; spacing widens toward mid-span where shear falls.
a.gu: Near the supports - shear force is maximum there; spacing widens toward mid-span where shear falls.

q.en: What is skirting and its usual height?
q.gu: What is skirting and its usual height?

a.en: The finish strip at the wall-floor junction (100-150 mm high) protecting the wall base from mop water and knocks; waterproofing turns up behind it in wet rooms.
a.gu: The finish strip at the wall-floor junction (100-150 mm high) protecting the wall base from mop water and knocks; waterproofing turns up behind it in wet rooms.

q.en: Name two door types and two window types.
q.gu: Name two door types and two window types.

a.en: Doors: panelled, flush (also battened, glazed, sliding). Windows: casement, sliding (also fixed, louvred, bay, pivoted).
a.gu: Doors: panelled, flush (also battened, glazed, sliding). Windows: casement, sliding (also fixed, louvred, bay, pivoted).

q.en: Why is the terrace (flat roof) waterproofing turned up at the parapet?
q.gu: Why is the terrace (flat roof) waterproofing turned up at the parapet?

a.en: Junctions leak first: turning the layer 150-300 up the parapet (with coping above) keeps the wall-roof corner sealed against driven rain and ponding.
a.gu: Junctions leak first: turning the layer 150-300 up the parapet (with coping above) keeps the wall-roof corner sealed against driven rain and ponding.
